inline.s: We read the scriptures and the treatises and teachings of the patriarchs and great masters for one purpose only: to seek the truth. Hence we must act from a true mind—taking things exactly as they are. Never, for the sake of private advantage, resort to the trick of quoting out of context, as when people twist the words “up to the end of one’s life, down to ten thoughts, none fail to reach rebirth” into the claim that “Master Daochuo said that if one merely recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a distracted mind in daily life (‘down to ten thoughts’), then at death one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (‘none fail to reach rebirth’). Therefore, calling the name brings certain rebirth.” The truth is that in the sentence preceding “up to the end of one’s life, down to ten thoughts, none fail to reach rebirth,” Master Daochuo had already made it crystal clear, “
only if one can fix the mind and apply it with single-minded concentration

.” Therefore, when one reads the two sentences in connection, “down to ten thoughts” refers to the ten thoughts of single-minded concentration at the moment of death (pure mindfulness continuing in an unbroken stream), not to the ten recitations of a distracted mind in daily life. To tear the text from its context in this way not only misleads others, but also harms oneself.

Another example: they claim that the “passage on the meaning of the essential vow” in Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: “If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions call upon my name and desire to be reborn in my land, down to ten thoughts—if they should not be reborn, I will not attain true enlightenment.” This, they say, means: “As long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a distracted mind in daily life (‘down to ten thoughts’), then at death one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (‘if they should not be reborn, I will not attain true enlightenment’). Therefore, calling the name brings certain rebirth.” This is nothing short of tearing the text from its context! Anyone who understands Master Shandao’s Pure Land teaching
will know that the “down to ten thoughts” spoken of by Master Shandao are the ten thoughts of an unbroken sequence of thoughts at the very end of life
. Master Shandao earnestly admonished, saying: “
It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because calling the name is easier than contemplation)
that continuation brings rebirth
If one can
keep thought following thought without interruption
, to the end of one’s life
, then of ten [practitioners] ten are reborn, of a hundred a hundred are reborn. ... May all people take this to heart: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must discipline the mind, restrain oneself, and never slacken by day or night
.” (See
Master Shandao: The Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao: Continuation Brings Rebirth
.) To tear the text from its context in this way not only misleads others, but also harms oneself.
Master Daochuo again gives this instruction in the Collected Teachings on Peace and Bliss:

Exhort all sentient beings: always keep right mindfulness present before them. A verse says: In the flower of youth, without affliction, if one is indolent and does not press on, greedily busying himself with worldly affairs and not cultivating giving, precepts, or meditation—when death at last swallows him, too late he repents and seeks to do good. The wise should observe and reflect, cutting off and eradicating the thoughts of the five desires. He who diligently trains the mind will have no regret at the end of life. When the mind is fixed and single, there arise no confused thoughts.
The wise who diligently gather the mind, at death their thoughts do not scatter. One who has not trained in single-mindedness, at death will surely be scattered.
When the mind is thus scattered, it is like training a horse with a millstone: when the time of battle comes, it only wheels in circles and will not run straight ahead.

All sentient beings are urged to make certain that right mindfulness is always present before them. The verse says: when one is in the prime of life, vigorous and free of affliction, if he is lazy and does not strive, and greedily runs after all manner of worldly affairs without cultivating giving, precepts, and meditation, then when death devours him it is too late to repent and seek to practice the good (the wholesome deeds spoken of here are the aforementioned “giving, precepts, and meditation”—charity, moral discipline, and meditative concentration). A wise person should be skilled at observing his own mind so as to cut off the deluded thoughts of the five desires. The one who diligently and single-mindedly trains the mind has no regret at death, because once the mind has become single and fixed by nature, there will be no confused thoughts at the end of life. Because the wise gather the mind diligently and with diligence in daily practice, their thoughts do not scatter at death. But one who has not trained the mind in single-mindedness will surely scatter at death. At that time, should the mind become scattered, you would wish to gather it but be unable; this is like using a millstone to train a horse—when battle comes, the horse only runs in circles and will not charge straight ahead.

The Five Desires. 1. Form, sound, scent, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to sweet and melodious tones; scent to fragrant odors; taste to delicious flavors; touch to agreeable tactile pleasures. Because these five can give rise to a mind of craving, they are therefore called the five desires. 2. The desire for wealth, the desire for sex, the desire for fame, the desire for food and drink, and the desire for sleep. The scriptures say: “Wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep are the five roots that lead to hell.” [Like training a horse with a millstone] It is like using a millstone to train a horse. “wèi” is the pronunciation of the word; it means a stone mill.
Question: How do “the ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death” differ from, and how are they related to, the “single-minded, unconfused state” spoken of in the Amitabha Sutra?

Answer: The ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death concern the time of dying, whereas the single-minded, unconfused state spoken of in the Amitabha Sutra refers to ordinary daily life (see the article
One-Mindedness, Unconfused

for details). The relation between the two is this: single-mindedness, unconfused, in daily life is the most dependable guarantee of the ten thoughts in succession at death—as the saying goes, “train the troops for a thousand days, use them for a single hour.” On this point Master Daochuo offers a vivid simile: a war horse must be given real combat training in peacetime. If in ordinary times it is trained by pulling a millstone, then at the time of battle it will only go round in circles and cannot charge into the enemy’s ranks. (Master Daochuo’s own words:

“The wise who diligently gather the mind, at death their thoughts do not scatter. One who has not trained in single-mindedness, at death will surely be scattered. When the mind is scattered, it is like training a horse with a millstone
(wèi, a stone mill)
. When the time of battle comes, it only wheels in circles and will not run straight ahead.”
Question: Why is it said that reciting the Buddha’s name is “the supremely easy path of practice”?

Answer: The practice of mindfulness of the Buddha need only achieve the success of contemplation, or the ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death, to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby escape birth and death and transcend the cycle of rebirth. In comparison with the ordinary path of practice, which requires the elimination of afflictions before one can escape birth and death and transcend the cycle, this is far, far easier—hence
the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is an easy path
. And the ten thoughts in succession at death are again much easier than the successful attainment of contemplation, so
reciting the Buddha’s name is the supremely easy path of practice

. One may say: those who cut off afflictions are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns, and those who succeed in contemplation are likewise rare and hard to find; but the ten thoughts in succession at death are something every person can accomplish through unremitting effort. Master Shandao said:
“Sentient beings are heavily burdened with hindrances; the object [of contemplation] is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness flutters and spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to achieve
(that is, contemplation is hard to accomplish)
. Therefore the Great Sage, in compassion,
(therefore Shakyamuni Buddha, in pity)
, directly urged us to call only upon the name. It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because calling the name is easier than contemplation)
that continuation brings rebirth
. If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, to the end of life, then of ten [practitioners] ten are reborn, of a hundred a hundred are reborn.”
(On the Mixed and the Exclusive Practice of Pure Karma)
[Contemplation] This refers to the thirteen contemplations in the Contemplation Sutra (Amitayurdhyana Sutra), such as the contemplation of the sun and the contemplation of water.
Question: Are the ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death very difficult? How can one accomplish the ten thoughts in succession at death?

Answer: The ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death can be attained by every person through unremitting effort; this is a path in which ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand reach rebirth. As for how one is to accomplish the ten thoughts in succession at death, see the article
The Ten Thoughts in Succession at Death, Continuation Brings Rebirth
Question:

The eighteenth vow (the original vow), the very root of the Pure Land school, has been given a very concise and lucid explanation by Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha (this is called the ‘passage on the meaning of the essential vow’),
as set out below
Master Shandao, in the ‘passage on the meaning of the essential vow’ of his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
says
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions call upon my name and desire to be reborn in my land,
down to ten thoughts
—if they should not be reborn, I will not attain true enlightenment.
Master Shandao, in the ‘passage on the meaning of the essential vow’ of his Method of Contemplation (Guan nian famen),
says
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions desire to be reborn in my land and call upon my name,
down to ten voices
, relying on the power of my vow—if they should not be reborn, I will not attain true enlightenment.
Master Shandao, in the ‘passage on the meaning of the essential vow’ of his Liturgy of Worship for Rebirth (Wang sheng li zan),
says
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions call upon my name,
down to ten voices

, if they should not be reborn, I will not attain true enlightenment. That Buddha has now appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood; you should know that this original vow is a weighty vow and not in vain—sentient beings who call upon and recollect him will surely attain rebirth.

In these three ‘passages on the meaning of the essential vow,’ it is said in each one that “down to ten thoughts” or “down to ten voices” will surely bring rebirth. This is to say: as long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a distracted mind in daily life, then at death one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, Master Shandao says: calling the name brings certain rebirth. Is this not so?
Answer: The ancients prized conciseness in their writing, so in understanding it one must always connect the preceding and the following text,
as well as the author’s overall thought,
and read them together—never take the words at face value, nor quote them out of context.
In the age of Master Shandao (
CE), owing to a series of teachings by Master Daochuo (
CE),
the understanding that “even to ten thoughts” in the eighteenth vow meant the ten thoughts in succession at death had already become an incontrovertible consensus,
so whenever “even to ten thoughts,” “down to ten thoughts,” or “down to ten voices” was mentioned,
everyone knew it referred to the ten thoughts in succession at death,
and so, when writing, there was no need to restate it. As for the meaning of the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo had already explained it very clearly in the Collected Teachings on Peace and Bliss:
If there is a sentient being who, even though he has done evil throughout his life,
at the moment of death, in ten thoughts continuing in succession,
calls upon my name, and is not reborn, then I will not attain true enlightenment.”
Here Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of “even to ten thoughts” in the eighteenth vow:
the ten thoughts in succession at the moment of death.
And, as related earlier, Master Daochuo gave a whole series of teachings on the ten thoughts in succession at death. Master Shandao himself, too, made it clear:
continuation brings rebirth
. Master Shandao says:
“It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because calling the name is easier than contemplation)
that continuation brings rebirth
If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, to the end of life
, then of ten [practitioners] ten are reborn, of a hundred a hundred are reborn.
May all people take this to heart:
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must discipline the mind, restrain oneself, and never slacken by day or night

(If Master Shandao truly advocated “calling the name brings certain rebirth,” why would he also say “keep thought following thought without interruption, to the end of life” and “whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must discipline the mind, restrain oneself, and never slacken by day or night”? Since the Original Vow path claims to rely upon Master Shandao, why do you not follow Master Shandao’s instruction “
keep thought following thought without interruption, to the end of life
” and “
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must discipline the mind, restrain oneself, and never slacken by day or night
”? On the contrary, why do you even proclaim that there is no need to practice? Is there truly no need to practice? Read the teachings and guidance of Master Shandao for yourselves!)
(See
Master Shandao: The Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao: Continuation Brings Rebirth
Furthermore, Master Shandao specially wrote the Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the End of Life, in order to stress that
right mindfulness at death brings rebirth
(see
Master Shandao: The Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the End of Life (annotated)

). The Original Vow path ignores these facts and twists the “down to ten thoughts” and “down to ten voices” spoken by Master Shandao into meaning ten recitations with a distracted mind in daily life, and from this concludes that Master Shandao said calling the name brings certain rebirth. But in fact Master Shandao plainly taught
“continuation brings rebirth,”
and
“right mindfulness at death brings rebirth.”

How can one so recklessly distort the facts? To study Buddhism, one must act from a true mind. The proverb says: “Covering one’s eyes to catch a sparrow is to deceive oneself.” Even a small creature cannot be won over by self-deception—how much less the great matter of birth and death!

[Covering one’s eyes to catch a sparrow] To cover one’s eyes while catching a sparrow, thinking that the bird will not see one. A metaphor for deceiving oneself. [Even a small creature cannot be won over by self-deception, how much less the great matter of birth and death] Catching a sparrow is a trivial matter, and yet it cannot be accomplished through self-deception; how much more so the great matter of escaping birth and death—how could it possibly be accomplished through self-deception? [Self-deception] To deceive oneself. The Original Vow path deceives itself: it thinks that by rewriting Master Shandao’s teaching of “continuation brings rebirth” into “calling the name brings certain rebirth,” one may recite the Buddha a little with a distracted mind in daily life and then be certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at death.
